name: Mise Migration Walkthrough
title: Pin CLI tools with mise instead of Homebrew
subtitle: Commit 945f6d7, 8 files. Docs excluded — the three files below are where behaviour changes. Hunks are ordered by when the machine runs them, not alphabetically: brew bundle, then mise install, then every login shell.

hunks.title: What Homebrew is still allowed to own
hunks.prose: Homebrew's job shrinks to four things it is the only one able to do: bootstrap (stow and mise itself — something has to run before mise exists), tools mise has no backend for, docker's CLI plugins, and GUI casks. Eight formulae that used to live here are deleted; they reappear as pins in the mise config two hunks from now.
annotated: Deletes git, gh, fzf, ripgrep, tree, tmux, neovim, tree-sitter, tree-sitter-cli from their old sections.
Re-adds git, tree, hf, audio-cpp under a new "No mise backend" heading — same formulae, new justification.
Keeps stow and mise as the bootstrap pair. mise's own version stays unpinned by construction.
Net: gh, fzf, ripgrep, tmux, neovim, tree-sitter leave Homebrew entirely.

diff.t: -brew "git"          # likely newer than the system git
+# stow links this package into $HOME (so it must exist before the mise
+# config does), and mise installs everything in config.toml. mise itself is
+# therefore the one tool whose version nothing pins -- documented in README.
+# ---- No mise backend (still unpinned; that gap is deliberate and visible) ----
+brew "git"                         # not in mise's registry (only git-* helpers)
+brew "0xshug0/audio-cpp/audio-cpp" # C++ audio inference engine powered by ggml

glosses.b: Symlink farm manager. Creates links from a package directory into a target (here $HOME), which is how dev/.config/mise/config.toml becomes ~/.config/mise/config.toml.
Three-part name: user/repo/formula. Required when the formula comes from a third-party tap rather than homebrew-core.

probe.q: Two formulae here are load-bearing for the whole scheme. Which two, and what happens on a fresh machine if either is missing?
probe.label: holds up
probe.answer:
stow and mise. The ordering claim in the comment is real and correct: stow links dev/.config/mise/config.toml into $HOME, so it must run before mise install has anything to read. The circularity is acknowledged rather than hidden — mise's own version is the one unpinned thing, which is the honest answer since a pinner cannot pin itself.

Worth carrying forward: git stays on Homebrew, and Homebrew here lives in ~/.homebrew. Remember that at hunk 6.

hunks.title: docker split across two managers
hunks.prose: The docker client moves to mise; buildx and compose stay on Homebrew, because they are not tools on PATH but plugins loaded from ~/.docker/cli-plugins, which a separate script symlinks out of the Homebrew prefix.
annotated: brew "colima" and brew "docker" removed — both become mise pins.
docker-buildx / docker-compose stay, with a comment explaining plugin resolution.
The comment concedes docker-compose does have a mise backend, and declines to move it to avoid teaching link-docker-cli-plugins a second source directory.
The old "Model tooling" section is folded into the no-backend section above.

diff.t: +# The docker *client* is pinned in mise. These two are not tools on PATH but
+# docker CLI plugins: `docker buildx` / `docker compose` resolve from
+# from this Homebrew prefix. docker-compose does have a mise backend, but
+# moving it would leave `docker compose` broken unless that script learned a
+# second source directory -- not worth the coupling for one formula.
+# docker-buildx has no mise backend at all.

glosses.b: Directory the docker client scans for `docker-<name>` executables, exposing each as a `docker <name>` subcommand. Not on PATH and not resolved through it.

probe.q: The docker client is now version-pinned and its plugins are not. What class of failure does that introduce that did not exist when both came from brew?
probe.label: design question
probe.answer:
Version skew between client and plugins. Before, brew bundle upgraded docker, docker-buildx and docker-compose together, so they moved in lockstep. Now the client is frozen at 29.7.2 while the plugins float on whatever Homebrew has today. Docker's CLI-plugin API is stable in practice, so this is unlikely to bite soon — but the reproducibility claim in the README is weaker than it reads: docker is pinned, docker compose is not.

Not a blocker. Worth one line in the README's "remaining unpinned" list, which names the plugins but not skew as the risk.

hunks.title: The pins themselves
hunks.prose: The receiving end. Eight CLI tools arrive with exact versions — no ranges, no latest — alongside the python runtime that was already here. This table is now the thing that determines what your shell resolves to.
annotated: New CLI tools section: 8 entries, each an exact version string.
Registry names differ from command names, hence the trailing comments: github-cli→gh, ripgrep→rg, neovim→nvim, docker-cli→docker.
docker-cli is deliberately the client-only backend, matching the plugin split left behind in the Brewfile.
The existing python = "3.12.14" is unchanged, just relabelled under a "Language runtimes" heading.

diff.t: +# ---- CLI tools (moved off Homebrew; see issue #4) ----
+tree-sitter  = "0.27.0"   # the CLI; :TSInstall compiles grammars with it
+docker-cli   = "29.7.2"   # the `docker` client only -- plugins stay in Brewfile

glosses.b: mise's registry key. The binary it puts on PATH is `gh`. Getting this key wrong fails at install time, not at use time — a cheap failure.
No range operator, so mise resolves this to precisely one upstream tag. If the tag does not exist, install fails hard rather than picking something near it.

tape.label: verified against upstream release tags — run 2026-09-04
tape.disc: Actually fetched from each project's GitHub releases API. Don't reason about whether a version string is plausible; go look.
rows: <ins>exists</ins> — one behind latest (v2.100.0). Fine; a pin is allowed to lag.
no such tag — latest tmux release is 3.7b (2026-07-01)

probe.q: Eight exact version strings, written by a model. One of them is not a real release. Which one — and when would you find out?
probe.label: real bug
probe.answer:
tmux = "3.7c". Upstream's latest is 3.7b; there is no 3.7c. Because the pin is exact with no fallback, mise install fails outright — so this breaks the very first ./reapply.sh on a clean machine, i.e. exactly the fresh-apply path this PR exists to make reliable.

The archetypal LLM-authored defect: format perfect, semantics invented, invisible to careful reading because 3.7c looks exactly as plausible as 3.7b. No amount of focus catches it. A four-line CI check does:

mise install --dry-run || exit 1

hunks.title: activate, and the precedence claim
hunks.prose: Runs on every login shell, after Homebrew's own snippet at 50-. The existing mise activate line is untouched; what's new is a comment asserting why the ordering matters — that activate prepends, so pinned tools beat leftover brew formulae of the same name.
annotated: No executable change in this hunk — comment only.
The claim: mise activate prepends the active tool paths, so ~/.local/share/mise/installs/… lands ahead of ~/.homebrew/bin.
This is the load-bearing assumption for the migration: it is what makes an un-uninstalled brew nvim harmless.

diff.t: -# mise: per-project language/tool version manager. Installs entirely in
-# userspace (~/.local/share/mise) — no sudo required either way.
+# mise: version manager for this account's CLI tools and language runtimes.
+# Installs entirely in userspace (~/.local/share/mise) -- no sudo either way.
# Numbered after 50-homebrew-isolated.zsh on purpose: mise is installed via
# Homebrew (see Brewfile), so ~/.homebrew/bin must already be on PATH here.
+# Being *after* it also matters for precedence -- `mise activate` prepends
+# the active tool paths, so a pinned nvim/gh/rg wins over a brew formula of
+# the same name that happens to still be installed.

glosses.b: Emits zsh code that prepends the active tools' bin directories to PATH and installs a precmd hook to re-resolve them when you cd into a directory with its own .mise.toml. Only affects shells that eval it.

tape.label: PATH, before and after this line
tape.disc: Illustrative shape — mise is not installed on the account I could reach, so this was not captured by trace-review.py. The ordering is what matters.

probe.q: The comment says ordering after 50-homebrew gives mise precedence. Is the ordering of these two files actually what determines precedence?
probe.label: comment is misleading
probe.answer:
Not really. mise activate prepends, so it wins regardless of whether it ran before or after the Homebrew snippet — prepending always beats an earlier prepend. The file ordering matters for a different, real reason, which the original comment already stated: mise is a brew-installed binary, so ~/.homebrew/bin must be on PATH for mise activate to be runnable at all.

The new sentence conflates "must run after, to exist" with "must run after, to win". Harmless today, but it is the kind of comment that gets cited later to justify a wrong change.

hunks.title: Shims appended as a fallback
hunks.prose: New block. Appends mise's shims directory to the end of PATH, deliberately not the front, so activate keeps priority. The stated purpose is to give non-interactive processes — a GUI launcher, a LaunchAgent — access to the pinned tools.
annotated: Guarded on the shims directory existing, so a machine where mise install hasn't run yet is unaffected.
export PATH="$PATH:…" — append, so anything already on PATH shadows the shims. Intentional per the comment.
Rationale given: processes started outside a shell that sources this file would otherwise see none of the pinned tools.

diff.t: +# Shims as a fallback, appended (not prepended) so activate keeps priority.
+# `mise activate` only rewrites PATH inside shells that source this file; a
+# process started outside one -- a GUI launcher, a LaunchAgent -- would
+# otherwise see none of the pinned tools.

glosses.b: $PATH comes first, so every directory already on PATH — including ~/.homebrew/bin — shadows the shims. They only take effect for a command that exists nowhere else.
Small executables named after each managed tool that re-exec the version mise resolves for the current directory. The alternative to rewriting PATH; works in processes that never ran `mise activate`.

probe.q: Read the justification, then the code. Does this block actually deliver what the comment promises?
probe.label: rationale doesn't hold
probe.answer:
No. The comment's whole premise is that this helps processes started outside a shell that sources this file — but such a process never sources this file, so the export never runs for it. On macOS, GUI apps launched from Finder or Dock inherit launchd's environment, not .zprofile. The block only ever executes inside exactly the shells that already ran mise activate one line above.

Where it does have an effect, it is the opposite of useful: appending puts the shims behind ~/.homebrew/bin, so for any tool present in both places the shim is dead code.

The real fix for the GUI case is launchctl config user path or a LaunchAgent, not a login-shell export. Either drop the block or correct the comment — as written, a future reader will trust a guarantee that isn't there.

hunks.title: The precedence tripwire
hunks.prose: The safety net: on every login, check that a few pinned tools actually resolve to the pinned copy, and print a yellow warning if one is being shadowed. Warn-only by design — a tool that simply isn't installed yet shouldn't be an error.
annotated: Loops over nvim rg gh tmux — four of the eight pinned tools.
whence -p does a PATH-only lookup, skipping aliases and functions. Correct choice for this check.
|| continue skips tools that aren't installed, honouring the warn-only intent.
The test for "shadowed": the resolved path does not start with $HOME.
Function is defined and invoked immediately, so it runs on every login.

diff.t: +# ... checks that tools this account pins actually resolve to the pinned
+# copy, rather than to /usr/bin. Warns only.
+  for tool in nvim rg gh tmux; do

glosses.b: Like `command -v` but PATH-only: ignores aliases, functions and builtins, so it reports the file that would actually be executed. The right primitive here.
Inside [[ ]] an unquoted right-hand side is a pattern, not a literal — so this is a prefix match on $HOME, not a string comparison. Intentional and correct zsh.

tape.label: what the guard returns for each plausible resolution
tape.disc: Hand-traced against the paths this account produces — mise isn't installed on the machine I could reach. The point is which rows stay silent.
rows: silent — correct, this is the pinned copy
<del>SILENT</del> — but this is a shadowing brew binary

probe.q: Recall where this account's Homebrew lives. Now re-read the shadowing test. What does it miss?
probe.label: real bug
probe.answer:
The guard is "$resolved" != "$HOME"/* — it fires only when a tool resolves outside your home directory. But this account's Homebrew prefix is ~/.homebrew, which is inside $HOME. So a leftover ~/.homebrew/bin/gh shadowing the pinned gh passes the check silently.

That is precisely the failure this PR is about. Every tool it just moved off Homebrew may still have a brew copy in ~/.homebrew/bin, and the tripwire built to catch that is blind to it. It catches only /usr/bin, where none of nvim/rg/gh/tmux ship.

Test against the mise install root instead:

[[ "$resolved" != "$HOME/.local/share/mise/"* ]]

Also: the loop covers 4 of 8 pinned tools. docker is unchecked and is the likeliest to have a stray copy.
